scenes.heading: Chemical bonding
scenes.say: Why does magnesium oxide melt at about two thousand eight hundred and fifty degrees, while table salt melts at eight hundred and one? The kind of bonding in a substance controls its properties. Let's look inside the bonds.
scenes.caption: Why does MgO melt at about 2850 °C, while NaCl melts at 801 °C? The kind of bonding in a substance controls its properties. Let's look inside the bonds.

scenes.heading: Ionic vs metallic bonding

left.title: Ionic
points: Big charge, small ions: strong lattice

right.title: Metallic
points: Cations in a sea of delocalised electrons

scenes.say: In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred and the ions sit in a lattice. Bigger charges and smaller ions give a stronger lattice, which is why magnesium oxide melts so high. In metallic bonding, electrons are pooled into a sea of delocalised electrons, so metals conduct and bend without breaking.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A tug-of-war: the stronger player pulls the rope their way
scenes.science: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair: δ− and δ+
scenes.breaks: a tug-of-war ends with a winner, but bond electrons settle into stable unequal sharing, and no bond is 100% ionic.
scenes.say: Bond polarity is like a tug-of-war, with the shared electrons as the rope. Equal players keep it in the middle: a non-polar bond. A stronger player shifts it their way: a polar bond. A much stronger player takes the whole rope, which is close to ionic. Bonding is a continuum.

scenes.heading: Formal charge
scenes.say: When several Lewis structures are possible, formal charge picks the best one. It's what an atom owns, minus what it keeps, minus half of what it shares. The best structure has charges near zero, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

scenes.heading: Worked example: bond energies
scenes.question: Estimate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (C–H 414, O=O 498, C=O 804, O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹).
scenes.say: Breaking bonds costs energy, and making bonds releases it, so delta H is roughly broken minus formed. For burning methane, the bonds broken add to two six five two, and the bonds formed add to three four six zero. So delta H is about minus eight hundred and eight kilojoules per mole.
scenes.caption: Breaking bonds costs energy, and making bonds releases it, so ΔH ≈ broken − formed. For methane, bonds broken = 2652 and bonds formed = 3460. So ΔH ≈ −808 kJ mol⁻¹.

scenes.heading: Hybridisation: count the domains
points: σ bond = head-on overlap (every bond has one)
π bond = side-on overlap of leftover p orbitals
scenes.say: Hybridisation is like a smoothie: blend one s and three p orbitals and you get four identical s p three cups. Count electron domains: four is s p three, three is s p two, two is s p. Hybrids make sigma bonds head-on, and leftover p orbitals make pi bonds side-on.
scenes.caption: Hybridisation is like a smoothie: blend one s and three p orbitals and you get four identical sp³ cups. Count electron domains: 4 is sp³, 3 is sp², 2 is sp. Hybrids make σ bonds head-on, and leftover p orbitals make π bonds side-on.

points: Covalent: a shared pair held by two nuclei
scenes.say: Quick recap. Ask: transferred, shared or pooled? Resonance structures describe one hybrid that never flips. Delta H is about bonds broken minus bonds formed. And count domains to find the hybridisation. Now try the practice questions!
